cells.tense: You are asking the question right now, in this moment, with the pen in your hand.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you already sense matters and tell someone why in one sentence — then let their answer land.
cells.core: You ask before you have the answer, and that doesn't rattle you. Something comes up — a person, a problem, a feeling — and you turn it over, look at it from the side, notice what doesn't quite fit. Working it that way is steady, and you don't need the conclusion to know you're close to one.\n\nBecause you're willing to not know yet, people bring you what they haven't sorted. That trust is doing real work in the room. Something in how you take a thing in makes its shape show up for whoever's standing nearby, and that part is worth keeping. The direction you're facing already has your name on it.
cells.sheetLine: You're curious in a way that shows other people what matters.
cells.verb: listening, discerning, and perceiving through fresh curiosity
cells.place: where you recognize what matters before you can say why

cells.tense: You are bracing for a future where you've finally understood enough, and you're already tired from that room.
cells.ask: Ask one question you don't already know the answer to, then stay quiet until the other person has finished answering.
cells.core: You run questions like a machine that has to produce the answer before anyone notices it doesn't have one. Every uncertainty gets chased, every stone turned, every possible reading held up at once — and you're bracing for the moment it all lands. It doesn't land. The pressure to understand ahead of time is flattening the curiosity that used to feel good.\n\nWhat changes it isn't more effort. Ask something you don't know. Not to be efficient — to find out. Curiosity doesn't need a deadline, and what you're actually after arrives on its own. Let one question sit unanswered and watch what shows up.
cells.sheetLine: You're chasing answers so hard the questions have stopped leading anywhere.

cells.tense: You are still standing in a doorway that closed behind you, waiting for permission to say what you already sense.
cells.ask: Write down one thing you notice about a situation you're in, without judging whether the notice is right.
cells.core: You sense things and don't act on it. Impressions arrive — a pull toward one person at the table, the feeling that someone isn't saying the whole truth — and you wave them off, waiting for more evidence, waiting for someone else to say it first. The fresh curiosity that would make you look closer is running on nothing. You carry a low tiredness that rest has stopped touching.\n\nIt isn't effort that starts this. Catch one plain impression and write it down as yours, without grading it. Let something small be seen. That's the move, and it works even if you're wrong about the impression — the writing is the practice, not the verdict.

cells.tense: The pen is already moving — you read rooms and people — and you keep calling it something other than your own judgment.
cells.ask: Name one read you've had this week and say out loud, 'That one was mine' — to yourself or to someone else.
cells.core: You read the room before anyone says a word. You feel the shift in a conversation before it turns, and your call lands often enough that people follow it. But you file it under being careful, being observant, paying attention. You're doing it while you work. You just aren't claiming it as something you did.\n\nSomething gets lost when you hand that credit away: you can't build on what you won't own. Saying "that one was mine" isn't arrogance — it's what makes the call usable the next time. Pick one moment from this week and stop filing it under coincidence. Let it count.
cells.sheetLine: You already read what matters. Try saying it was you.
